metadata.title: Learning Mathematics for Life: A Perspective from PISA (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD report chapter uses PISA 2003 mathematics assessment data from 15-year-olds sampled within participating countries. The chapter describes the overall PISA cycle (framework development, field trials, sampling, main study implementation, data cleaning, and reporting) but does not provide a chapter-level specification of the exact student weight variable(s) used in the analyses reported here. The analyses focus on item-level and country-level patterns (e.g., percent correct, item difficulty on the PISA scale, and comparisons of relative item difficulty by content, context, competencies, and item format), rather than on estimating population-representative means for a single regression model. As a result, the manuscript does not document whether complex survey weights were applied in the specific computations shown; analysts using the PISA international database should follow the PISA technical documentation for applying the appropriate sampling weights and replicate weights when producing standard errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The chapter does not report an empirical predictive model with a PV-based cognitive achievement dependent variable; instead it provides framework descriptions and item-level/country-level analyses (e.g., percent correct, item difficulty logits, and comparisons across item characteristics). Because the dependent outcomes discussed are not PV-based achievement scores in a model-based estimation context, PV handling is not applicable. Missing data handling is also not specified at the analytic-strategy level for an ML/PV estimation procedure; the chapter discusses omission rates and how missing responses are treated as incorrect for scoring, but it does not document a formal missing-data imputation/deletion strategy for an analysis dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The chapter describes PISA 2003 as testing 15-year-olds sampled from participating countries, with the mathematics domain as the major focus in the 2003 cycle. It does not specify a chapter-level analytic subsample restriction (e.g., grade-only, school-type-only, or item-only filtering) for the reported descriptive/item-difficulty analyses. The analyses are described as using the PISA mathematics item set and released items, and in some places referencing field trial coding for omission-rate analyses; where specific item sets are discussed (e.g., released items in Annexes, or subsets by content/context/competency), the filtering is by item characteristics rather than by student eligibility.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD chapter provides an assessment-framework and item-characteristics perspective on PISA 2003 mathematics rather than training or evaluating machine-learning models. It explains how PISA defines mathematical literacy (mathematical literacy as functional use in real-world contexts) and structures the domain using the “ML + 3Cs” model (content, context, competencies), including competency clusters (reproduction, connections, reflection) and four overarching content ideas (change & relationships, space & shape, quantity, uncertainty). The chapter then illustrates how item difficulty is quantified using percent-correct, logit-based item difficulty, and the PISA mathematics scale (mean 500, SD 100) with six proficiency levels. It reports descriptive comparisons showing that question difficulty varies systematically with competency cluster, traditional curriculum topic, context type, word count (reading load), and item format, and it discusses omission rates as a function of item difficulty and format. Methodologically, it emphasizes scoring conventions (missing responses treated as incorrect for scoring) and notes limitations of PISA’s time constraints for observing the full “mathematisation” cycle.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a framework/assessment-design and descriptive analysis chapter, not an empirical ML paper with a predictive target and reported model performance. As a result, there is no ML algorithm evaluation, no PV-based dependent-variable modeling, and no documented student-level analytic sample size or per-country N for the chapter’s analyses. The chapter’s evidence is presented through item-level difficulty metrics, percent-correct summaries, and comparisons across item characteristics and country patterns, which explains the sparse ML- and sample-specific fields.
